sources.news_title: Putin Agrees to Resume Talks with U.S., Ukraine
sources.text:
by Ben Whedon
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday agreed to participate in talks with the U.S. and Ukraine in a bid to end the war in Eastern Europe.
Putin advisor Yuri Ushakov confirmed that Moscow had agreed “in principle” to negotiations on Nov. 10, according to the Associated Press. His commitment follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressing openness to a ceasefire on the current front lines of the conflict.
But there is little to suggest that Russia’s terms to end the war have changed and that resumed negotiations will make headway. Notably, Russia and the U.S. have negotiated a series of deals in recent weeks, including for the release of political prisoners and the injection of Russian diesel into global markets.
Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on X that he and Jared Kushner “met with Russian, Ukrainian, and European leaders to advance President Trump’s mission to end the war.”
“In St. Petersburg, we met with President Putin to build on the progress made in Oslo with President Zelenskyy, discuss a peace framework, and thank President Putin for releasing American citizen Stephen Hubbard to return home to his family. These discussions were constructive, and will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level,” Witkoff said.
“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace that will provide security and prosperity for generations to come,” he added.
It also comes in the wake of Putin suggesting President Donald Trump personally meet with him and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss an end to the war in a summit that would not include Zelensky.
The war began in February of 2022 over Russian concerns about Ukraine’s potential entry into NATO. Conflict between Moscow and Kyiv, however, has persisted since 2014, when pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych was ousted in the Maidan Revolution.
– – –
Ben Whedon is a reporter for Just the News. Zachery Schmidt is the digital editor of The Star News Network and contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
sources.text:
Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has held talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.

Putin Agrees to Renew Peace Talks With Ukraine and US as President Trump Pushes to End War
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way peace negotiations with the United States and Ukraine, marking a new diplomatic development in President Trump’s efforts to end the war that has devastated Eastern Europe for more than four years.
The agreement emerged Wednesday following a three-hour meeting between Putin and Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace outside St. Petersburg.
Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov confirmed that Putin had agreed in principle to restart negotiations after November 10, potentially bringing representatives from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv back to the negotiating table for the first time since February.
The proposed discussions would take place at the technical level, meaning government representatives and specialists would negotiate rather than the three countries’ presidents meeting directly.
Officials indicated that Abu Dhabi could host the negotiations, which would focus on establishing security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine following a potential peace agreement.
The development follows months of stalled diplomacy and growing pressure from President Trump for both countries to reach a settlement.
Witkoff arrived in Russia after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and several European leaders in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday.
Those discussions focused on developing a framework for ending the conflict, including security guarantees for Ukraine and arrangements intended to prevent renewed fighting.
Witkoff described the Oslo meetings as productive and expressed optimism that diplomatic efforts were beginning to regain momentum.
“There is some degree of momentum,” Witkoff said ahead of his meeting with Putin.
The American envoy presented proposals developed during the Oslo discussions and urged Russia to consider restarting direct negotiations with Ukraine and the United States.
Putin’s agreement represents a procedural step forward, although substantial disagreements remain over the conditions required to end the war.
Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly failed to reach a settlement because of disputes involving occupied territory, military deployments and security guarantees.
The Kremlin has demanded concessions that Ukraine has resisted, while Kyiv has insisted that any agreement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible safeguards against future Russian attacks.
Ushakov said the proposed negotiations would concentrate on developing a security framework for both countries once the fighting ends.
However, the Kremlin also expressed reservations about the proposals brought from Oslo.
Ushakov said the documents contained little of immediate value toward resolving the conflict, although he later acknowledged that they represented movement in a potentially constructive direction.
The mixed assessment demonstrates that Russia’s willingness to participate in talks does not necessarily mean Putin is prepared to accept the conditions sought by Ukraine.
President Trump has made ending the conflict a central foreign policy priority, repeatedly emphasizing the enormous loss of life and financial cost of the war.
The president has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian leader of failing to pursue a negotiated settlement aggressively enough.
Speaking at the White House on Tuesday, Trump again called on Ukraine to reach an agreement.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters.
The president pointed to the substantial military and financial assistance Washington has provided Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss,” Trump said.
He also warned that Ukraine could face serious consequences if the conflict continues without a negotiated settlement.
The latest diplomatic effort comes as Zelensky has signaled some willingness to consider freezing the conflict along existing battle lines as a starting point for peace.
In an interview broadcast Wednesday on Fox News, the Ukrainian president said a freeze in fighting could provide the foundation for ending the war.
“Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” Zelensky said.
Such an arrangement could involve halting military operations without immediately resolving the competing territorial claims that have complicated previous negotiations.
Ukraine has nevertheless insisted that any lasting agreement must include security guarantees capable of preventing Russia from launching another invasion.
Zelensky has also maintained that the most difficult questions would ultimately require direct negotiations between national leaders.
Putin’s latest agreement falls short of committing to a personal meeting with Zelensky or President Trump.
Instead, the Kremlin has accepted a return to lower-level discussions that could establish the groundwork for future negotiations.
Previous rounds of American-mediated talks took place in Abu Dhabi and Geneva earlier this year.
Those meetings produced limited progress beyond prisoner exchanges, with both sides maintaining their central demands.
The renewed diplomatic push also produced a separate development involving an American citizen imprisoned in Russia.
Putin agreed to release Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher who had been held by Russian authorities for more than four years.
Hubbard was detained after Russian forces seized territory in eastern Ukraine in 2022 and was subsequently convicted by a Russian court of serving as a mercenary.
The American government had sought his release, and President Trump personally raised the matter with Putin.
Russia released Hubbard as Witkoff arrived for Wednesday’s negotiations.
Trump said the release occurred without the United States being required to exchange a Russian prisoner.
The president welcomed the development, describing it as an important achievement for an American citizen and his family.
The release was viewed as a diplomatic gesture accompanying the renewed discussions between Washington and Moscow.
Economic issues were also addressed during Witkoff’s meeting with Putin.
The American envoy thanked Russia for lifting restrictions on diesel exports, a decision that could help ease pressure on international fuel markets.
American farmers and transportation companies have been struggling with high diesel prices, prompting the Trump administration to pursue additional energy supplies.
Putin also expressed interest in discussing the possible restoration of economic relations between Russia and the United States.
The Kremlin said the two sides reviewed potential commercial projects and opportunities for future cooperation.
Those discussions come amid disagreements over sanctions and whether economic engagement with Moscow could encourage progress toward ending the war.
Putin additionally offered to discuss the ongoing conflict involving Iran, suggesting that Russia could use its longstanding relationship with Tehran to assist diplomatic efforts.
The Kremlin also raised the possibility of a meeting involving Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the American president’s expected visit to China next month.
No agreement for such a summit has been announced.
The possibility of broader diplomatic talks has generated concern in Ukraine, where officials have insisted that decisions about their country’s future must include Ukrainian participation.
Zelensky has warned against negotiations that would allow other major powers to determine Ukraine’s future without Kyiv’s involvement.
Despite the diplomatic developments, fighting continued across Ukraine on Wednesday.
Russian attacks struck residential areas and energy infrastructure, killing at least five people and injuring more than 20 others, according to Ukrainian officials.
Authorities in Kyiv reported three deaths and extensive damage to residential buildings following overnight strikes.
Additional attacks near Kharkiv killed two people and injured several others.
Russia also reported intercepting hundreds of Ukrainian drones over its territory and surrounding regions.
The continuing attacks underscore the distance between an agreement to negotiate and an actual ceasefire.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv has announced a halt to military operations, and the proposed talks remain weeks away.
Nevertheless, the decision to restart negotiations provides President Trump’s administration with another opportunity to pursue a diplomatic settlement.
Witkoff is expected to continue consultations with Ukrainian and European officials as Washington works to narrow the differences between the two sides.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also been involved in coordinating American diplomatic efforts and discussing the proposed framework with Ukrainian representatives.
The administration’s immediate objective is to establish a negotiating process that can address territorial disputes, security arrangements and the conditions necessary for ending hostilities.
For now, Putin’s agreement represents renewed diplomatic engagement rather than a completed peace deal.
The next major test will come after November 10, when representatives from the United States, Russia and Ukraine could return to negotiations.
After more than four years of war and repeated failed diplomatic efforts, President Trump’s administration is attempting to turn the latest opening into substantive progress toward ending the conflict.

- Putin agreed to resume the negotiations “in principle,” according to his foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov.

The discussion in St. Petersburg lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said, and came a day after Witkoff met with Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
The proposals from the Oslo meeting “contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis,” Ushakov said.

Putin said he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia economic ties, adding that he was also prepared to discuss the U.S.-led conflict with Iran. Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Ushakov said that “large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation” between Russia and the U.S. were discussed in detail with Witkoff.
“Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage,” he said.

Putin also met Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St. Petersburg for talks with other Russian officials, the Kremlin said.
Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a U.S. proposal for U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Putin and Witkoff also discussed a possible meeting next month between the Russian, Chinese and U.S. leaders at an economic summit in China, Ushakov said, adding that Beijing is already preparing for it.

Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo early Wednesday, where he visited Norway's parliament and met with lawmakers.
Zelenskyy said the talks in Oslo and St. Petersburg included discussion of future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction and the possibility of a ceasefire.
Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
Russian attacks kill 5 people and wound at least 23 others, Ukraine says
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 wounded, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 others were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said that overnight its forces struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

sources.news_title: Putin Signals Willingness to Resume Ukraine Peace Negotiations After November 10 Following US Talks
sources.text:
Russia has agreed in principle to return to three-way peace negotiations with Ukraine and the United States, opening a possible diplomatic path toward ending the war as continued attacks and disagreements over territory complicate efforts to secure a ceasefire.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed in principle to resume direct negotiations involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington after Nov. 10, marking a new development in President Donald Trump’s efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine after more than four years of fighting.
The announcement followed approximately three hours of discussions Wednesday, Oct. 21, between Putin and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace near St. Petersburg. Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said Russia was prepared to return to the trilateral negotiating format, with discussions expected to concentrate on security arrangements for both countries following a potential settlement.
The decision represents a possible opening after months of limited diplomatic progress, although no formal meeting date or agreement on the terms of a ceasefire has been announced.
Ushakov said Putin had accepted the proposal “in principle” and that negotiations could resume after Nov. 10, according to reporting on the Kremlin’s announcement.
The proposed discussions would focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.
The framework would bring representatives from the United States, Russia and Ukraine together to address unresolved questions involving territorial control, military arrangements and the guarantees needed to prevent another conflict.
Witkoff arrived in Russia carrying proposals developed during consultations with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European officials in Oslo the previous day. The American envoy sought to determine whether Moscow would accept renewed direct negotiations after previous diplomatic initiatives failed to bridge the differences between the warring countries.
During televised remarks at the beginning of Wednesday’s meeting, Witkoff urged Putin to consider bringing representatives from all three governments back to the negotiating table. He suggested that technical working groups could address detailed questions while political leaders continued discussing the broader settlement.
According to Axios, which reported on the latest diplomatic initiative, Witkoff presented documents outlining possible approaches to ending the conflict and requested Putin’s consideration of the proposals.
The Kremlin’s subsequent announcement indicated that Moscow was willing to examine the renewed negotiating format, but significant disagreements remain over the conditions Russia and Ukraine would accept.
Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to resolve the conflict as the meeting began. Russian foreign policy adviser Ushakov and presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev participated in the discussions, while Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner was expected to contribute through a remote connection.
Witkoff characterized his earlier consultations in Norway as productive and expressed optimism that the latest diplomatic contacts could help restart negotiations.
“There is some degree of momentum,” Witkoff said before his meeting with Putin.
The envoy’s visit to St. Petersburg followed talks Tuesday involving Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and representatives of several European governments.
Those discussions examined possible ceasefire arrangements, territorial questions, postwar reconstruction and the security commitments Ukraine would require before agreeing to a negotiated settlement.
Stubb said the Oslo meeting “made genuine progress,” reflecting cautious optimism among European officials involved in the discussions.
The Finnish president’s assessment did not indicate that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed on substantive terms. Rather, it suggested that Ukraine, the United States and participating European governments had made progress toward developing a coordinated proposal for further negotiations.
Zelenskyy has maintained that halting the fighting must be the immediate objective of any renewed diplomatic effort.
In an interview broadcast Wednesday by Fox News, the Ukrainian president said freezing the conflict along existing military lines represented the minimum acceptable step toward ending the war.
“Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” Zelenskyy said.
The statement reflects Kyiv’s attempt to secure a cessation of hostilities before addressing more difficult questions involving territories occupied by Russian forces.
Russia continues to demand concessions that Ukraine has resisted, including recognition of Russian territorial claims and restrictions on Ukraine’s future military relationships with Western countries.
Moscow has repeatedly insisted that any settlement must address what it describes as the underlying causes of the war, including its objections to Ukraine’s possible membership in NATO.
Ukraine maintains that Russia’s invasion violated its sovereignty and that any agreement must include enforceable protections against renewed military aggression.
These opposing positions have repeatedly prevented American-led diplomatic initiatives from producing a comprehensive settlement.
Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has pursued direct contacts with Moscow and Kyiv, arguing that a negotiated agreement is necessary to end the casualties and economic destruction associated with the war.
The president has also increased public pressure on Zelenskyy, criticizing the Ukrainian government for failing to reach terms with Russia despite substantial American assistance.
During remarks at the White House on Tuesday, Trump called on the Ukrainian leader to accept an agreement.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
Trump warned that continued resistance to a settlement could produce additional consequences for Ukraine.
If an agreement is not reached, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” the president said.
His comments came amid renewed concerns in Kyiv over the administration’s approach to military assistance, intelligence sharing and economic relations with Russia.
Ukraine has continued requesting reliable warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks, particularly as Moscow intensifies strikes against electricity infrastructure and other civilian facilities.
Zelenskyy recently expressed concern that Ukrainian forces were not receiving sufficient advance notice from Western partners before certain Russian strikes.
After discussions with American officials, including a telephone conversation with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Kyiv reported that some early-warning information had resumed.
The dispute illustrates the importance of Western intelligence support to Ukraine’s defenses and the difficulty of separating military cooperation from broader diplomatic disagreements.
The latest peace initiative also follows an Oct. 11 announcement by Trump that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking one another’s energy infrastructure.
That understanding has not prevented continued strikes against power facilities, oil installations and other energy-related targets.
Russian forces launched another series of attacks overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, striking residential and energy infrastructure in several Ukrainian cities.
Kyiv’s military administration reported that three people were killed and 12 others wounded in the capital, where strikes damaged 10 residential buildings.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three additional cities during the latest Russian operations.
Outside Kharkiv, near the country’s northeastern border with Russia, drone strikes killed two people and wounded 11 others in a residential area, according to Ukrainian officials.
The attacks occurred as diplomats were preparing to discuss possible mechanisms for ending the fighting, underscoring the difference between progress at the negotiating table and conditions on the battlefield.
Ukraine has continued conducting long-range strikes against Russian military and energy targets.
Over the weekend, Ukrainian drones attacked facilities near St. Petersburg, igniting fires at an oil export terminal and a storage depot.
Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones toward Russian territory Sunday in one of its largest aerial operations since the war began, according to reports concerning the assault.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones overnight Tuesday and Wednesday across multiple Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.
Moscow also reported strikes against Ukrainian military and transportation targets, including a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier traveling toward the port of Odesa.
The competing accounts of military activity could not be independently verified in their entirety, and both sides have continued reporting attacks despite the renewed diplomatic discussions.
The persistence of hostilities remains a central obstacle to negotiations because each government is attempting to improve or preserve its military position while discussions continue.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov acknowledged the possibility of reviewing new American proposals Tuesday but cautioned against expectations of a rapid settlement.
Lavrov said Moscow was willing to consider Washington’s ideas but did not anticipate any “miracle” emerging from the diplomatic effort.
The cautious assessment contrasted with the more optimistic comments made by some European officials following the Oslo meeting.
Norwegian Prime Minister Støre said the recent exchanges might indicate that Russia was becoming more receptive to diplomatic engagement.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.
Støre also confirmed that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for additional consultations after completing his discussions in Russia.
Zelenskyy remained in Norway on Wednesday, visiting the Norwegian parliament and meeting lawmakers as Ukraine sought continued European political and military support.
The diplomatic efforts are taking place alongside changes in Washington’s economic relations with Moscow.
During Wednesday’s meeting, Witkoff thanked Putin for lifting Russia’s restrictions on diesel exports, a development that the Trump administration has associated with efforts to reduce fuel prices in the United States.
The American envoy said increased diesel availability could benefit American farmers and trucking companies facing elevated operating expenses.
The arrangement has attracted criticism from lawmakers concerned that renewed energy trade could provide Russia with additional revenue while its military operations in Ukraine continue.
Trump has also moved to ease certain sanctions affecting Russia, prompting questions about whether Washington is reducing economic pressure on Moscow before securing concessions on the battlefield or at the negotiating table.
Supporters of the administration’s approach argue that economic engagement may create opportunities for negotiation, while critics contend that reducing sanctions could weaken incentives for Russia to end the war.
Putin used Wednesday’s discussions to express interest in restoring broader economic relations with the United States.

Moscow: Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed Wednesday, October 21, to resume trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kyiv on ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said.
The Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the talks after November 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters following a meeting in St Petersburg between Putin and US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.
The trilateral talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.
Witkoff’s talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine came as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
As the talks began, Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war. The discussion lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said.
Trump’s effort to end war have made no significant progress
Witkoff’s visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway’s capital, Oslo.
Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to US-led peace efforts, more than 4½ years after Russia’s army launched an all-out invasion. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough.
Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.
However, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said late Tuesday, October 20, that the Oslo meeting, which he attended, “made genuine progress.”
Zelenskyy said that freezing the conflict in Ukraine was the “minimum” required from Russia to bring about an end to the war.
“Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” Zelenskyy said in an interview broadcast Wednesday on Fox News.
Witkoff sees some degree of momentum’ in peace efforts
Witkoff and Putin met at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, with Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table. Witkoff said Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, was due to join the discussion via a video link.
Before the talks, Witkoff said that he would inform Putin about Tuesday’s meeting in Oslo, which he described as “productive,” adding that “there is some degree of momentum.”
He thanked Putin for lifting Russia’s ban on diesel exports, which angered some US lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for US farmers and truckers.
Putin said that he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of US-Russia economic ties, adding that he’s also prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Russia on Wednesday released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, Witkoff said, in what appeared to be a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin after Trump asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard.
Putin was also due to meet Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St Petersburg meeting with other Russian top officials, the Kremlin said.
Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Norway’s prime minister sees a possible new phase’ in talks
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he visited Norway’s parliament and met with lawmakers.
Witkoff appeared to be making another attempt at overcoming hurdles that have kept a deal out of reach.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction and the possibility of a ceasefire.
Trump said October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure. But Russia has kept hammering Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.
Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new US proposals about Ukraine, but he doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington.
At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Russian attacks kill 5 people and wound 25 others, Ukraine says
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 wounded, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 others were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defence Ministry said that overnight its forces struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defence Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

sources.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said.
The Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the talks after November 10, Mr Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters following a meeting in St Petersburg between Mr Putin and US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.
The talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends”, Mr Ushakov said.
Mr Witkoff’s talks with Mr Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine came as Mr Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has insisted that only a summit of leaders can break the impasse. The two armies remain locked on the battlefield, and the two countries pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.
Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of negotiations earlier this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.
However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war as Moscow and Kyiv stuck to their basic demands.
The discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said, and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelensky and some European leaders in Norway’s capital, Oslo.
The proposals from the Oslo meeting “contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis”, Mr Ushakov said.
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow is not “fully satisfied” with the Oslo proposals, they are a step in the right direction.
Mr Witkoff’s meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to US-led peace efforts, more than four years after the war began. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress.
Mr Zelensky said freezing the conflict in Ukraine was the “minimum” required from Russia to bring about an end to the war.
“Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” Mr Zelensky said in an interview broadcast on Wednesday on Fox News.
Mr Witkoff and Mt Putin met at St Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table. Mr Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link, Mr Ushakov said.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that “there is some degree of momentum” in talks.
During the meeting, Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner proposed a three-way meeting with the US, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level and shared progress on their talks with Mr Zelensky a day earlier, according to a US official familiar with the talks.
Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US, after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US politicians, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and lorry drivers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of US-Russia economic ties, adding that he was also prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran. Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said.
Mr Ushakov said that “large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for co-operation” between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
“Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage,” he said.

Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran.

“I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Mr Store told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.
Mr Zelensky was still in Oslo early Wednesday, where he visited Norway’s parliament and met politicians.
Mr Zelensky said the talks in Oslo and St Petersburg included discussion of future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, post-war reconstruction and the possibility of a ceasefire.
At the White House on Tuesday, Mr Trump increased the pressure on Mr Zelensky to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again.
“We want Zelensky to make a deal,” Mr Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
If that does not happen “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing”, Mr Trump said.
Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Mr Zelensky said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies.
Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 injured, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city’s military administration said.
Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said.
The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces overnight struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
The Russian Defence Ministry reported on Wednesday that its air defences overnight intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black Sea.

sources.news_title: Russia agrees to resume negotiations with Ukraine and the United States after November 10
sources.text:
PUTIN AGREES TO MORE TALKS—UKRAINE IS STILL WAITING FOR HIM TO STOP THE WAR
Another meeting. Another proposal. Another Russian promise to consider more talks.
After Steve Witkoff met Putin near St. Petersburg on October 21, the Kremlin said Russia had agreed “in principle” to resume negotiations with Ukraine and the United States after November 10.
Apparently, the Kremlin’s most reliable production line remains the manufacture of future meetings.
Witkoff brought proposals developed following discussions with Zelenskyy and European partners in Oslo. Moscow’s announcement offers a possible next step, but no ceasefire has been announced and no settlement agreed.
Ukraine has already offered reciprocal restraint on energy strikes. Russia has rejected a separate energy truce. That refusal matters more than another carefully worded expression of willingness to negotiate.
Talks can serve a purpose. They can also give Moscow more time while its forces continue attacking. Until Russian commitments produce observable changes, there is ample reason to question whether this is diplomacy advancing—or another round of delay.
Russia also released Stephen Hubbard, the 74-year-old retired American teacher whom Washington had designated wrongfully detained. His freedom is welcome news. He deserves to return to his family, recover and live beyond the prison walls where he should never have been held.
With the U.S. midterms approaching, Trump gains a favorable headline from that release. The political benefit is clear; it does not establish his private motive or turn Hubbard’s homecoming into evidence of Russian progress toward peace.
Welcome home, Stephen.
Now the administration must demand results for the Ukrainians still living under Russian attack. Putin has demonstrated that he can release a prisoner when he chooses. He must now demonstrate a willingness to stop the killing—not simply reserve another date to discuss it.

sources.news_title: Putin Peace Negotiations: Major Shift After US Talks
sources.text:
St Petersburg, Russia, 21 October, (Brussels Morning Newspaper) – Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed in principle to restart trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States after 10 November, raising hopes of renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war. The development marks a significant step in Putin peace negotiations, although major disagreements remain over territory and security guarantees.
The announcement followed Wednesday’s meeting between Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St Petersburg. Washington is seeking to revive discussions after previous attempts failed to produce a comprehensive settlement.
Kremlin Confirms Readiness for November Peace Talks
Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov confirmed Moscow’s willingness to return to negotiations following the meeting.
According to Ushakov, Putin agreed in principle to resume the three-way discussions after 10 November, with particular attention to establishing security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine following the conflict.
However, officials have not announced a final date, location or agreed negotiating agenda.
The Russian position signals a willingness to reopen diplomatic channels but does not represent acceptance of a ceasefire or a final settlement.
US Envoy Presents Fresh Proposals to Putin
Witkoff travelled to Russia after participating in discussions in Oslo on 20 October with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European representatives.
The Oslo consultations addressed security guarantees, economic reconstruction, energy infrastructure and possible arrangements for reducing hostilities.
During his meeting with Putin, Witkoff presented documents outlining potential approaches to a negotiated settlement.
He also proposed restarting negotiations between technical teams representing Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The discussions form part of President Donald Trump’s continuing diplomatic efforts to secure an agreement ending the conflict.
Putin’s Position on Ukraine Remains Unchanged
Despite the renewed diplomatic opening, Russia and Ukraine remain divided over several fundamental issues.
Moscow continues to oppose Ukrainian membership of NATO and seeks recognition of its territorial demands.
Kyiv maintains that any settlement must protect Ukrainian sovereignty and provide credible guarantees against renewed military aggression.
Speaking in an interview broadcast on Wednesday, Zelenskyy supported freezing the fighting as a practical starting point for ending the war.
Neither side has accepted a comprehensive agreement, and military operations continue.
European Leaders Assess the Diplomatic Opening
The possible resumption of Putin peace negotiations carries significant implications for Brussels and European governments supporting Ukraine.
The European Union has provided financial, military and humanitarian assistance while maintaining sanctions against Russia.
A future settlement could affect European defence commitments, reconstruction funding, sanctions policy and the continent’s long-term security arrangements.
Previous US-led diplomatic initiatives have struggled to reconcile Russian territorial demands with Ukraine’s position on sovereignty.
The UK House of Commons Library has identified territorial disputes and security guarantees among the principal obstacles to an agreement.
What Happens After 10 November?
Further consultations are expected between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv to determine whether formal negotiations can resume in November.
Officials must establish the participants, location and scope of any renewed discussions.
Technical teams could examine ceasefire arrangements, territorial questions and future security guarantees if the proposed talks proceed.
For now, Putin’s agreement represents a potential diplomatic opening rather than a confirmed peace breakthrough.
Whether negotiations produce measurable progress will depend on the willingness of all parties to address the unresolved issues that have prevented earlier agreements.
